p: Codex Alexandrinus leaves out "were not filled"; Swete prints it from Codex Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, from Codex Venetus (V)
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it

why: Without the verb the question has no main verb at all, so A has lost the words by a copying slip. Swete supplies them from V, and the Plain follows his text.

a: The old man was led away, his head thick with gray hair.
t: One old man, or a crowd of old men?
p: Codex Alexandrinus has "an old man full of gray hair"; Codex Venetus "a crowd of old men, gray-haired."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: an old man full of gray hair, thickly covered
readings.plain: The old man was led away, his head thick with gray hair.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: a crowd of old men, gray
readings.plain: A crowd of gray-haired old men was led away.

why: The Plain follows Swete's text, which takes the old man as one figure standing for many. V's plural makes the same point openly; Brenton's English ("a multitude of aged hoary-haired men") follows that reading. Both codices then have a plural participle (pepykasmenōn), so the verse was disturbed early.

a: This was not for the forced labor mentioned a little earlier.
t: Not for labor, or for labor?
p: Codex Venetus turns the denial into a statement: the register was for forced labor.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: οὐκ εἰς τὴν ἔμπροσθεν βραχεῖ προδεδηλωμένην τῶν ἔργων κατὰ τρόπον λατρείαν
readings.en: not for the service of labor shown a little before
readings.plain: This was not for the forced labor mentioned a little earlier.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: for (it was) for the toilsome service
readings.plain: It was for the hard labor mentioned a little earlier, and

why: A's reading fits the next clause, "but so that they could be tortured," which needs a "not" before it. V's "for" and "toilsome" look like a scribe smoothing a hard sentence.

a: , and he said things against God that were not fit to be said.
p: Swete adds "God" in brackets; Codex Alexandrinus has no object, and Codex Venetus lacks the whole clause.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with τὸν θεόν supplied in square brackets
readings.orig: εἰς δὲ [τὸν θεὸν] τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα λαλῶν
readings.en: and speaking against [God] what was not fitting
readings.plain: , and he said things against God that were not fit to be said.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it
readings.orig: εις δε τα μη καθ. λαλων
readings.en: and speaking against (or "to") things not fitting
readings.plain: , and he said things that were not fit to be said.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. His bracket shows that he supplied "God" for the sense; A's Greek has no object for "against" (eis), and V lacks the clause. Brenton's English (1851) reads "against the Greatest God."

p: Swete prints systrophias, "gathering"; Rahlfs and the lexicon read syntrophias, "being raised together."

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition; Liddell-Scott-Jones (LSJ) calls Swete's word here a false reading for this one
Swete's printed text (his notes give no other reading for A or V)
readings.plain: who are bound up with me

why: The Plain departs from Swete here. Systrophia barely exists as a word: LSJ lists it at this verse as a false reading for syntrophia, "being raised together," which Rahlfs prints. The two words differ by one letter. Brenton's English (1851) has "familiar friendship" and Emmet's (1913) "our life together."

p: Codex Venetus adds a word: the king is testing his Kinsmen as if they were senseless.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: how long will you test us so

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.plain: keep testing us as if we had no sense

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. V's extra word (spelled oddly, allogous, for alogous, "senseless") is behind Brenton's "as of men bereft of reason."

a: bring down in fire and leave empty
p: Both codices have the letters prēn. Swete restores "having burned"; Rahlfs prints "laid flat ... empty."

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition (and Emmet's 1913 text, which he takes from later manuscripts)
readings.en: laid flat by fire ... empty of those who sacrifice
readings.plain: bring down in fire and leave empty

readings.w: Swete's printed text: πρή[σα]ν[τα], his restoration of πρην in A and V; A and V also lack ἔρημον, "empty"
readings.en: having burned with fire ... (no word for 'empty')

why: The Plain departs from Swete here, because his text does not make sense. Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Venetus have only prēn, which is not a word in this place. Swete fills it out as prēsanta, "having burned," but, as Emmet (1913) noted, the uncials also lack "and" and "empty," so the end of the verse still has no meaning. Rahlfs's text (prēnea, "laid flat," with erēmon, "empty") gives a whole sentence. Either way the king swears to destroy the temple by fire. Emmet thought the verse had been conflated from two readings.

p: Codex Alexandrinus garbles the last words of the verse; Swete prints them from Codex Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with Codex Venetus (V)
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it

why: A's letters helkontai all are a miscopying of helkonta gala, "drawing milk." Swete's notes also show that A and V first had a masculine participle (echontes) for the mothers holding the babies, corrected in V to the feminine. The Plain follows Swete.

a: well known among the Jews of the countryside
p: Codex Venetus makes Eleazar "well known among the priests of the country."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: ἐπίσημος τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χώρας Ἰουδαίων
readings.en: notable among the Jews from the country
readings.plain: well known among the Jews of the countryside

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; Brenton's English ("an illustrious priest of the country")
readings.plain: well known among the priests of the countryside

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. V's "priests" may come from the priestly name Eleazar, or from the memory of other priestly Eleazars; Brenton's English follows it.

p: In Codex Alexandrinus a later hand wrote "under Pharaoh" over an erasure where Swete prints "Father, you, Pharaoh."

readings.w: Swete's printed text
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), corrected by a later hand over an erasure, as Swete's notes report it

why: The corrector's "under Pharaoh" does not fit the sentence, whose verb is "you destroyed" with Pharaoh as its object. Swete's "Father, you" matches the form of the other rescues, which each begin "you" (6:5, 6, 7), and the prayer's address to God as Father (6:8).
b: The Plain's "there was Pharaoh" does not keep the Greek's "you" (sy) at the head of each rescue (6:4, 5, 6, 7); English needs the verb first. The "you" comes back in each verb: "You destroyed him," "You, Master, broke him," and so on.

a: You made the red-hot furnace wet with dew, and you rescued them,
p: Codex Venetus has no dew: "you rescued them from the furnace burning so long."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: having bedewed the fiery furnace, you rescued
readings.plain: You made the red-hot furnace wet with dew, and you rescued them,

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: from the long-burning fiery furnace you rescued
readings.plain: You rescued them from the furnace that had burned red-hot so long,

why: The Plain follows A and Swete. A's "dew" matches the Greek additions to Daniel 3, where the angel makes the middle of the furnace like a pneuma drosou, a "wind of dew" (Greek Daniel 3:50 in Swete's text; the site's Daniel variant at 3:23 sums it up as "a moist wind"). Emmet (1913) called 3 Maccabees 6:6 "the apparent quotation" of that passage; the shared image shows that the writer probably knew it, though one image is not proof. Brenton's English (1851) has "a dewy coolness." V's "long-burning" may be a scribe's change of an unusual verb.

p: Codex Venetus calls God "Protector of all" instead of "Judge of all."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: Both words fit the prayer: God judges the arrogant and protects the weak. The Plain follows Swete's text.

p: Codex Venetus leaves out "the Gentiles": "Let it be shown to all."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD)); also Rahlfs
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. The prayer has just asked that "the Gentiles cower" (6:13), so "all the Gentiles" fits; V's shorter text makes the same request of everyone. The contrast with Leviticus 26:44 ("the land of their enemies") is the same either way.

p: Codex Alexandrinus has "time" (chronon), Swete prints "dance" (choron) with a corrector of Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with the corrector of Codex Venetus (Va)
readings.en: having formed the dance already mentioned

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it

why: The words differ by one letter. "The dance we spoke of" points back to 6:32, where the Jews "formed dances"; A's "the time we spoke of" has no clear reference, so it is a copying slip.

p: Codex Venetus has "our affairs" (pragmata) for "our decrees" (prostagmata).

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: κατευθύνοντος ἡμῖν τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ τὰ προστάγματα
readings.en: the great God directing our decrees

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: V's "affairs" is the usual phrase of royal letters (compare 3:13, "so are our affairs"). A's "decrees" is the harder reading and fits the irony: the God who now guides the king's decrees is undoing the first one. The Plain follows Swete.

p: Codex Venetus says they "punished" the renegades, not that they "killed" them.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: Both codices agree in the next clause that "they put them to death" (anēiroun), and both say three hundred were killed (7:15), so V's softer verb does not change the event. The Plain follows Swete.

p: Swete's text reads "holy Savior." Alexandrinus has "of the holy ones, to you," and Venetus "eternal."

readings.w: Swete's printed text
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: of the holy ones, to you

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it (αιωνιω for Swete's ἁγίῳ); Rahlfs's edition prints αἰωνίῳ σωτῆρι, and Emmet's (1913) and Brenton's (1851) English have "the eternal Savior"

why: A's letters (hagiōn soi) look like a miscopying of hagiōi sōtēri, which Swete prints. Swete's note sets V's aiōniōi against the two words hagiōi sōtēri, but Emmet's notes give V's word as a replacement for "holy" alone, and Rahlfs prints "eternal Savior"; so V keeps "Savior." The Plain follows Swete's text.

t: Rescue and release, or the enjoyment of rescue?
p: Codex Venetus has "full enjoyment of rescue" for "full rescue and release."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it (with εἰληφότες, "having received"); so also Rahlfs and Emmet (1913)

why: The two readings differ by a few letters (apolysin, "release"; apolausin, "enjoyment"). Swete's text puts two nouns side by side with no "and," which is hard Greek; V's is smoother, and Rahlfs and Emmet follow it. The sense is close: the faithful have come through to full rescue. The Plain follows Swete.

p: Codex Alexandrinus breaks off at "each to the"; the Plain follows Codex Venetus, "each to his own."

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; so also Rahlfs's edition and Emmet's (1913) and Brenton's (1851) English
readings.en: each to his own (home); and very great (goes with 7:21)

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))

why: A's sentence has lost words: "each to the" runs straight on into "before, among the enemies" (7:21), which makes no sense. Emmet (1913) explained the loss: a scribe's eye jumped from eis tēn to the like ending of pleistēn. V supplies "his own" and, for 7:21, "very great." The Plain follows V here, and so does the next verse (see 7:21).

a: They had very great authority in the sight of their enemies
p: This reading goes with 7:20. Codex Venetus has "very great" authority; Alexandrinus only "before"; Rahlfs adds "than."

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it (καὶ πλείστην at the end of 7:20; V also lacks ἐν)
readings.orig: και πλειστην εμπροσθεν τοις εχθροις εξουσιαν
readings.en: and very great authority before the enemies
readings.plain: They had very great authority in the sight of their enemies

readings.w: Rahlfs's edition; Emmet's (1913) and Brenton's (1851) English
readings.orig: καὶ πλείστην ἢ ἔμπροσθεν ἐν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἐξουσίαν
readings.en: and much more authority than before among the enemies
readings.plain: They had far more authority than before among their enemies

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.plain: Before, they had authority among their enemies

why: Without V's words A's text is not a sentence. The Plain renders V as Swete reports it. "More than before" needs the small word ē, "than," which Rahlfs prints; Emmet's notes show that V does not have it, so the comparative belongs to the later witnesses and editors, not to V. V's wording is known only from Swete's short note, so the exact sentence cannot be fully recovered.

p: Swete and Codex Alexandrinus have "payment" (phorou); Codex Venetus "fear" (phobou), one letter apart.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; so also Rahlfs's edition and Emmet's (1913) and Brenton's (1851) English

why: Both readings make sense, so the Plain keeps Swete's text. Phoros is "tribute" or, in general, "any payment" (LSJ): those who held the Jews' goods gave them back with a heavy payment besides. V's "fear" fits 7:21 ("with glory and awe") and the picture of enemies who fear the rescued (compare Esther 8:17), and most editors and translators prefer it. That is an argument, not proof; the two words differ by one letter, and either could have come from the other.

t: The great God or the Most Great God?
p: Codex Venetus has "the Most Great God," the book's usual title.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; also Rahlfs

why: "The Most Great God" (ho megistos theos) is one of the book's fixed titles (see 1:16 and 5:25), and V may have brought this verse into line with it; A's "great God" matches 7:2. The Plain follows Swete.
